title: Evaluating the Computational Advantages of the Variational Quantum Circuit Model in Financial Fraud Detection
abstract_summary: The paper investigates variational quantum circuit (VQC) classifiers for financial fraud detection using a real Intesa Sanpaolo transactions dataset reduced via PCA to fit NISQ-era simulation limits. VQC models on ideal simulators outperformed several classical baselines (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, SVM, neural networks) in precision and recall on reduced datasets, but tests on IBM quantum hardware showed that current device noise substantially degrades practical performance.
methodology_description: The study evaluates Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) classifiers for fraud detection on a real-world bank transaction alert dataset. The original dataset (≈515k records, 15 features, ≈2% fraud) was preprocessed (normalization) and reduced by PCA to 2, 4, 6, and 8 principal components and by stratified sampling to dataset sizes of 1k, 2k, 4k, 6k, 8k, 10k and 20k while preserving the fraud/legit ratio. Each reduced dataset was split stratified into train/validation/test (80/10/10). The VQC is implemented as a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline using angle encoding (various RX/RY/RZ and Hadamard combinations), two ansatz choices (Basic Entangling Layer and Strongly Entangling Layer), optional re-uploading (data encoding repeated between param layers), measurement of the most significant qubit via Pauli-Z plus a trainable bias and sigmoid to produce a probability, and training with a classical optimizer. Binary cross-entropy loss was minimized using Adam (lr 0.01) in PyTorch, with mini-batch training (batch size 10) for 10 epochs. For each reduced dataset a large hyperparameter sweep (400 models per reduced dataset across encodings, ansatz, layers, re-uploading, etc.) was performed. Model selection used the area under the precision–recall (PR) curve on validation to pick the best encoding/ansatz/layers; threshold tuning was performed by evaluating 50 threshold values (in (0,0.5]) and selecting the threshold maximizing F_{β} (β=2) on validation. Final evaluation on test reports precision and recall. Classical baselines (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM linear & RBF, Neural Network) were trained and compared under the same train/val/test regime. Most quantum experiments were run on the PennyLane default.qubit simulator (Legion HPC) and selected models were submitted to IBM quantum devices (ibm_brisbane and ibm_algiers) to assess noise impact; fidelity (Hellinger) and Kullback–Leibler divergence between simulator/device outputs were also measured.
algorithms_used: Support Vector Machine (linear and RBF kernels)
experimental_setup: Most experiments executed on the PennyLane default.qubit simulator on the Legion HPC server (HPC@POLITO). Classical model training and local prediction performed on an Intel Xeon Gold 6134 CPU (single-process) with ~103 GB RAM. Selected VQC circuits were executed on IBM real quantum devices ibm_brisbane (127 qubits) and ibm_algiers (27 qubits) via IBM Quantum Runtime Services (Pay-as-you-go plan).
dataset_used: Real transaction alert dataset provided by Intesa Sanpaolo: 515,651 entries from 2022 with 15 features (5 numerical: transaction timestamp, amount, year, month, day; 11 categorical features hashed with SHA-512). Class imbalance: ≈2% fraud. Dataset reduced by normalization + PCA (2,4,6,8 components) and stratified sampling to sizes {1000,2000,4000,6000,8000,10000,20000}. Split stratified into 80% training, 10% validation, 10% test.

key_findings: [supported] On ideal quantum simulators, Variational Quantum Circuits (VQCs) showed, on average, better classification quality in terms of precision and recall than several classical baselines (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, Neural Networks) on the reduced, PCA-processed subsets of a real bank-transaction dataset.
[supported] The study used a real Intesa Sanpaolo transaction-derived dataset (≈515k entries, 15 features, fraud rate ≈2%) and performed PCA; eight principal components capture >99% of the variance.

[supported] For experimentation feasibility, dataset size and feature dimension were reduced (samples: 1k–20k; PCA components: 2,4,6,8) and 400 different models were trained per reduced dataset to select best architectures/hyperparameters.

[supported] Angle encoding (and more complex angle-encoding variants, e.g., multiple rotation gates and Hadamard pre-layers) and deeper/more expressive ansatz generally yielded better VQC validation performance in this study; re-uploading is an effective model hyperparameter (sometimes beneficial, sometimes not).

[supported] When executed on current noisy IBM hardware (ibm_brisbane and ibm_algiers), the trained VQCs suffered severe degradation: noise destroyed the simulator-observed precision/recall advantages (ROC/PR curves collapsed), and fidelity/KL-divergence analyses showed significant deviations from ideal simulator outputs.

[supported] Logistic Regression behaved as the strongest classical baseline among those tested for these reduced datasets, while XGBoost often performed worse in terms of area under precision-recall in validation.

[speculative] Quantum machine learning can leverage superposition and entanglement to represent more complex decision boundaries than classical models and therefore could provide practical advantages for highly imbalanced classification tasks like fraud detection.
[supported] The authors made their trained quantum models available in a public GitHub repository (facilitating transfer-learning and further evaluation).
[supported] Measurement on the most significant qubit using Pauli-Z plus a trainable bias and sigmoid output was an effective readout strategy in the implemented VQC pipeline.

[supported] The experimental workflow (training on PennyLane default.qubit simulator with PyTorch/Adam, BCE loss, mini-batches of 10, 10 epochs) and threshold tuning (F-beta with beta=2) were key components of model selection/evaluation.

[speculative] The paper suggests that VQC/model design choices (encoding type, ansatz, number of layers, re-uploading) are problem-dependent and must be treated as hyperparameters—i.e., there is no one-size-fits-all VQC for fraud detection.
[supported] PCA dimensionality reduction plus stratified subsampling were necessary to make simulation-based QML experiments tractable given classical simulator exponential scaling.

[speculative] The authors propose future directions (alternative dimensionality reduction methods like tensor-train networks, other encodings e.g., amplitude encoding, QSVMs, hybrid QC-classical optimizers, QUBO-based training) as promising avenues—these are presented as recommendations rather than demonstrated results.
[supported] The study empirically demonstrates that, under current NISQ noise levels, potential simulator-observed quantum advantages do not translate to existing real quantum devices.
results_summary: This empirical study trained and evaluated VQC-based quantum classifiers (angle-encoded, various ansatz, with/without re-uploading) on PCA-reduced subsets of a real bank-transaction dataset and compared them to classical baselines. On ideal quantum simulators the VQCs frequently achieved superior precision and recall (the figures of merit most relevant for imbalanced fraud detection) compared to Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, and Neural Networks across many reduced-dataset configurations. More expressive encodings and deeper ansatz often improved VQC performance. However, when the same circuits were run on current IBM quantum hardware (ibm_brisbane/ibm_algiers), noise eliminated the simulator-era advantages; measured outputs diverged substantially from ideal simulations (low fidelity / high KLD), demonstrating that practical deployment on contemporary NISQ devices is not yet viable. The work thus reports a simulator-level empirical advantage but cautions that hardware noise precludes real-device advantage today.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper presents simulator-based empirical evidence that VQCs can outperform several classical models in precision and recall on PCA-reduced subsets of a real fraud dataset. However, the advantage is observed only in ideal simulations; real-device noise on current NISQ hardware destroyed the benefit. Therefore any claimed quantum advantage is provisional and contingent on ideal/noiseless execution or future hardware improvements.
limitations: Dataset dimensionality and size were reduced (via PCA and sampling) to make simulation tractable; original dataset (~515k entries, 15 features) could not be used directly.
Main quantum experiments were run on an ideal simulator (Pennylane default.qubit) due to NISQ noise and limited reliability of current quantum hardware.
Real-device tests (ibm_brisbane, ibm_algiers) showed that device noise severely degraded model performance compared to the simulator.
Categorical features were hashed (SHA-512) for privacy, causing loss of information and reduced interpretability.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used for feature reduction, which reduces interpretability of the transformed features.
The study focused primarily on angle encoding for VQC; other encoding schemes were not exhaustively evaluated in the main experiments.
The paper concentrates on the Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) model; other QML approaches were not deeply explored in experiments (e.g., QSVM, quantum graph NN).

Simulation complexity grows exponentially with qubit count, limiting the number of qubits (hence features) and transactions that could be simulated (practical upper bound used was 8 PCA components and up to 20k samples).

Gradient/backpropagation used for training is only applicable in simulation; different gradient-evaluation methods (e.g., parameter-shift) are required on hardware, complicating direct hardware training.
Re-uploading (data re-encoding) increases circuit depth and hence sensitivity to noise on real devices.
Threshold optimization was constrained to the (0, 0.5] range and a discrete grid of values (50 points), which may limit detection of other potentially optimal thresholds.
Evaluation used a single institution's dataset (Intesa Sanpaolo); external validity / generalizability to other banks/datasets was not established.
The study reports performance-focused metrics (precision/recall/Gmean/Fβ) but does not provide detailed runtime/resource-cost comparisons between quantum simulations and classical training.
[inferred] The results achieved on the simulator may not generalize to production settings because real NISQ devices currently cannot reproduce the simulator performance.
[inferred] The hyperparameter choices for training (10 epochs, batch size 10, Adam lr=0.01) and the limited training regime may be insufficient for fully converged classical or quantum models.
[inferred] Class imbalance handling relied primarily on threshold optimization rather than exploring resampling, weighting, or cost-sensitive learning strategies.
[inferred] The experimental design used a train/validation/test split but did not report extensive cross-validation; risk of overfitting or variance in model selection remains.
[inferred] Model interpretability (particularly for VQC) is limited, which may be an obstacle in financial applications requiring explanations and regulatory compliance.
[inferred] Reproducibility and external access to the exact datasets are restricted; dataset access requires agreement with Intesa Sanpaolo, limiting independent replication.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — On ideal (noise-free) simulators, VQC classifiers outperformed multiple classical baselines (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, SVM, neural network) in precision and recall on PCA-reduced transaction datasets.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The study uses a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline: classical preprocessing (normalization, PCA, stratified sampling), classical optimizer (Adam) to train parameterised quantum circuits, and threshold tuning for imbalanced classification.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments on IBM quantum devices (ibm_brisbane, ibm_algiers) show substantial degradation from device noise (measured via Hellinger fidelity and KLD), indicating the simulator advantage does not translate to current NISQ hardware.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Extensive hyperparameter sweeps (≈400 models per reduced dataset) and threshold tuning were used to robustly select VQC variants and demonstrated consistent simulator-side gains across several reduced dataset sizes and PCA dimensions.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Necessity of dimensionality reduction (PCA to 2–8 components) and stratified downsampling to small dataset sizes to fit NISQ circuit sizes highlights practical constraints for real-world deployment.
contradictions: Simulator vs device performance contradiction — While the paper demonstrates a clear simulator-based advantage of VQCs over classical baselines, execution on real IBM hardware shows noise causes large performance drops and distributional divergence (Hellinger/KLD). This contradicts claims that quantum models providing simulator gains will yield practical advantages on contemporary hardware.

Scalability contradiction — The need to reduce 15 original features via PCA to at most 8 components and to heavily downsample the dataset to sizes manageable for training contradicts claims of immediate scalability of VQC approaches to full-size financial datasets; the study shows preprocessing compromises (dimensionality reduction & sampling) are required to fit NISQ constraints.
